Review
Recent progress in density functional theory 
and machine learning for predicting MXene 
properties
Mokhtar Hjiri1,*  and Nazir Mustapha1
1 Department of Physics, College of Sciences, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), 11623 Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
ABSTRACT
Recent years have seen remarkable progress in the integration of Density Func-
tional Theory (DFT) calculations and Machine Learning (ML) techniques, par-
ticularly within the realm of materials science. This review delves into this bur-
geoning field, focusing on their application to MXenes, a significant family of 
two-dimensional (2D) materials comprising transition metal carbides, nitrides, 
or carbonitrides. MXenes have garnered attention for their remarkable proper-
ties and versatile applications, including catalysis, gas sensing, and energy stor-
age. We further investigate the integration of ML methodologies, utilizing vari-
ous algorithms to predict MXene properties with high accuracy and efficiency. 
Through a comprehensive literature analysis, we underscore the synergistic rela-
tionship between DFT calculations and ML approaches, showcasing how their 
combined use accelerates MXene discovery and optimization for diverse techno-
logical applications. Additionally, we discuss current challenges and future direc-
tions in leveraging these computational techniques to advance our understanding 
and utilization of MXene materials. This review serves as a valuable resource for 
researchers at the intersection of computational methods and materials science, 
offering insights into state-of-the-art techniques for predicting MXene proper-
ties, performance, and guiding future research endeavors in this dynamic field.
Introduction
The rapid advancement of two-dimensional materials 
has significantly reshaped the landscape of modern 
materials science, enabling breakthroughs in energy, 
electronics, and environmental technologies. Follow-
ing the pioneering work on graphene, extensive efforts 
have been devoted to the synthesis, processing, and 
functionalization of 2D materials using scalable tech-
niques such as printing and additive manufacturing, 
which have facilitated their integration into flexible 
and wearable devices [1 , 2]. In parallel, the develop-
ment of 2D semiconductor nanosheets has opened 
new opportunities in photocatalysis and solar energy 
conversion, highlighting the critical role of dimen-
sionality in tailoring material properties [3 ]. Among

attracted considerable attention due to their outstand-
ing physicochemical properties and versatile applica-

nanocomposites has demonstrated significant poten-
tial in energy storage, catalytic systems and conver-
sion systems, enabling enhanced performance through 
controlled composition and structure [4 ].
Furthermore, MXenes have shown exceptional 
promise in sensing technologies, particularly in elec-
trochemical sensors and biosensors, owing to their 
high conductivity and surface functionality [5]. Recent 
advances in computational and data-driven methodol-
ogies have further accelerated materials discovery, as 
demonstrated by machine learning-assisted design of 
high-performance functional materials for biomedical 
applications [6 ]. In Fig. 1 we illustrate the significant 
advancements in both DFT calculations and machine 
learning techniques for predicting MXene potential 
from 2018 to 2025. We observe a steady increase in 
progress metrics for both methodologies over the 
years, reflecting the continuous evolution and refine-
ment of computational methods in MXene research. 
From the figure, it is evident that recent years have 
witnessed notable advancements in DFT calculations 
and machine learning approaches for understand-
ing and predicting MXene properties. This progress 
underscores the growing importance of computa-
tional techniques in MXene research and highlights 
the potential for further breakthroughs in the future.
Beyond materials design, the integration of machine 
learning into engineering systems has enabled pre-
dictive modeling in complex environments, such as 
real-time prediction of geological properties using 
physics-informed neural networks [7]. Similarly, data-
driven approaches have been successfully applied to 
optimize demand-side management in smart energy 
systems, improving efficiency and reliability [8 ]. In 
environmental applications, advanced predictive 
models have enhanced precipitation nowcasting by 
integrating multiphysical parameters, demonstrat-
ing the power of combining physical understanding 
with data-driven techniques [9 ]. At the atomic scale, 
computational simulations such as molecular dynam-
ics have provided insights into interfacial processes, 
including ion desorption mechanisms on mineral sur-
faces [10]. Additionally, machine learning models have 
been increasingly utilized in biomedical engineering, 
for instance in predicting hemodynamic states using 
multi-feature fusion approaches [11]. Optimization 
algorithms, such as adaptive differential evolution 
strategies, have further improved the performance of 
numerical and engineering models by effectively navi-
gating complex solution spaces [12].
The application of data-driven methodologies 
extends to large-scale infrastructure systems, includ -
ing the assessment of supply reliability in natural gas 
pipeline networks [13] and the optimization of engine 
performance in dual-fuel systems [14]. In marine and 
underwater environments, lightweight machine learn-
ing models have been developed for acoustic localiza-
tion, demonstrating improved real-world applicabil-
ity through knowledge distillation techniques [15]. 
Meanwhile, understanding material degradation and 
corrosion mechanisms remains essential for ensur-
ing long-term stability, as highlighted by studies on 
molten metal interactions with structural materi-
als [16]. Integrated data-driven frameworks have 
also been proposed for managing supply–demand

Recent breakthroughs in nanomaterials synthesis, 
such as the fabrication of high-quality black phos-
phorus nanoribbons with controlled edge structures, 
have further demonstrated the importance of atomic-
level precision in tuning material properties [20 ]. In 
parallel, significant efforts have been directed toward 
developing efficient catalysts for  CO2 hydrogenation 
and sustainable fuel production, particularly using 
non-noble metal systems [21]. Advances in carbon 
capture technologies have also been achieved through 
the development of novel catalysts and porous mate-
rials, including molecular sieves and metal–organic 
frameworks with tailored functional sites for efficient 
 C O2 adsorption and separation [22, 23]. Furthermore, 
interfacial and solvation chemistry in electrochemical 
systems has been shown to play a crucial role in deter-
mining performance, especially in advanced battery 
technologies [24]. The design of novel alloys, includ-
ing high-entropy systems, has also contributed to the 
development of materials with enhanced mechanical 
and functional properties [25].
Within this broader context, MXenes have emerged 
as a highly versatile platform for energy conversion 
and storage applications, offering unique advantages 
such as high conductivity and tunable surface chemis-
try [26]. Fundamental studies have revealed the critical 
role of surface effects in determining the structural, 
electronic, and mechanical properties of MXenes, 
providing essential insights into their behavior at the 
atomic scale [27]. Advances in fabrication techniques 
have enabled the development of both two-dimen-
sional and three-dimensional MXene-based nano-
materials for energy and environmental applications 
[28]. Moreover, the influence of surface terminations 
and morphology on catalytic performance has been 
extensively investigated, particularly in the context of 
hydrogen production and photocatalysis [ 29]. Inter -
face engineering has also been identified as a key fac-
tor in enhancing energy storage and conversion per-
formance, highlighting the importance of interfacial 
chemistry in MXene-based systems [30].
Significant progress has been made in the devel-
opment of MXene-based nanocomposites for electro-
chemical energy storage, including supercapacitors 
and batteries, where improved performance has been 
achieved through synergistic material design [31]. 
Comprehensive studies have further explored the 
status and future perspectives of MXenes in energy 
storage applications, emphasizing their potential for 
next-generation technologies [32]. However, the vast 
compositional space and structural complexity of 
MXenes present significant challenges for traditional 
experimental and computational approaches. In Fig. 2, 
we depicted the most important aspects of MXenes, 
including their applications [33].
To address these challenges, computational and 
data-driven methods have become indispensable tools 
in modern materials science. The integration of quan-
tum mechanical calculations with machine learning 
has enabled efficient molecular and materials design, 
significantly reducing computational costs while 
maintaining high accuracy [34, 35]. Recent advances 
in computational tools and data-driven modeling have 
further enhanced the ability to predict and optimize 
material properties across a wide range of applications 
[36, 37]. First-principles methods, particularly Density 
Functional Theory (DFT), remain a cornerstone of 
computational materials science, providing detailed 
insights into mechanical, electronic, and structural

Considering the above developments, this review 
aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic 
overview of recent progress in Density Functional 
Theory and Machine Learning for predicting MXene 
properties. Specifically, this work seeks to bridge the 
gap between fundamental theory and practical appli-
cations by integrating insights from experimental 
studies, computational modeling, and data-driven 
approaches. The objective is to (i) summarize the 
current understanding of MXene materials and their 
diverse applications, (ii) critically analyze the role of 
DFT in elucidating their structural, electronic, and 
catalytic properties, (iii) examine the emerging role 
of machine learning in accelerating MXene discovery 
and property prediction, and (iv) highlight the syner-
gistic integration of DFT and ML as a transformative 
approach for high-throughput screening and materials 
informatics. Furthermore, this review identifies cur-
rent challenges and outlines future research directions 
to guide the development of next-generation MXene-
based materials for energy, environmental, and tech-
nological applications.
MXenes: structures, properties, 
and applications
Introduction to MXenes
MXenes constitute an intriguing class of materials 
that have garnered immense interest in the scientific 
community due to their remarkable properties and 
versatile applications. These materials, denoted by 
the general formula  Mn+1XnTx, where M represents a 
transition metal, X denotes carbon or nitrogen, and 
 Tx signifies surface functional groups (e.g., -OH, -F, 
H, S or -O), are derived from their bulk counterparts 
known as MAX phases [41–43]. MAX phases, with the 
general formula M n+1AXn, are layered ternary com-
pounds composed of transition metals (M), group A 
elements (typically early transition metals or post-
transition metals), and carbon or nitrogen (X) [44–46]. 
The distinguishing feature of MAX phases is their 
unique crystal structure, which consists of alternat-
ing layers of transition metal carbide or nitride and 
A-group elements. The ‘ A’ layers are often composed 
of elements such as aluminum, silicon, or gallium. 
The process of selectively etching the ‘ A’ layers from 
MAX phases under appropriate conditions leads to the 
formation of MXenes, which exhibit distinct layered 
structures with intriguing properties. MXenes typi-
cally feature transition metal carbide or nitride lay-
ers interspersed with intercalated functional groups, 
such as hydroxyl or fluorine terminations. This lay-
ered arrangement imparts MXenes with exceptional 
mechanical flexibility and high surface area, making 
them attractive candidates for various applications 
[47–50]. Figure 3 showcases six distinct MXene for-
mulas, each representing a unique stoichiometry and 
layer arrangement. The  M2X configuration embodies 
a fundamental MXene structure with a single transi-
tion metal layer flanked by two X layers, presenting a 
straightforward yet inherently functional composition 
(e.g.,  Mo2C) [51]. In contrast, the  M2XO2 configuration 
(e.g.,  Mo2CO2) introduces an additional oxygen layer 
between each transition metal layer, enhancing func-
tionality and facilitating applications in energy storage 
and catalysis [52, 53]. The M’2M”X2 configuration (e.g., 
 C r2NbC2) involves the juxtaposition of two different 
transition metals with one X layer between them, offer-
ing customizable properties suited for specific appli-
cations [54]. In M’2M”2X3 (e.g.,  Cr2Nb2C3), two transi-
tion metal layers are interspersed with three X layers, 
yielding a more intricate structure conducive to ion 
storage and sensing [55]. M’2M”X2O2 features identical 
transition metal layers separated by an oxygen layer 
(e.g.,  Cr2NbN2O2), providing enhanced stability and 
electrochemical properties suitable for batteries and 
capacitors [56]. Finally, M’2M”2X3O2 (e.g.,  V2Cr2C3O2) 
combines two different transition metal layers with 
three X layers and an additional oxygen layer, amal-
gamating diverse elemental properties for multifunc-
tional applications.
Structural characteristics of MXenes
MXenes, characterized by their layered structure 
composed of transition metal carbide or nitride layers 
separated by intercalated functional groups, epito-
mize versatility in material design [57]. These func-
tional groups, encompassing hydroxyl or fluorine 
terminations, intricately modulate MXene surface 
chemistry, enabling tailored interactions crucial for 
diverse applications [58]. This structural diversity 
underpins MXenes’ exceptional mechanical flexibility,

Computational studies on MXenes
Introduction to computational methods
In the realm of computational chemistry, density 
functional theory stands as a cornerstone, enabling 
the numerical solution of the Schrödinger equation to 
unravel the intricacies of quantum systems [81, 82]. 
This process involves breaking down the equation 
into discrete components, allowing for computational 
analysis via algorithms. From this solution emerges a 
wealth of information, including the electronic wave 
function and density, which delineates the behav-
ior and spatial distribution of electrons within the 
system. Leveraging these insights, various physical 
quantities pertinent to the system’s ground state can 
be extracted, offering crucial understanding of stabil-
ity, reactivity, and molecular geometry. Furthermore, 
DFT computations unveil the distribution of atomic 
charges within molecules, crucial for predicting inter-
molecular interactions in chemical reactions. Beyond 
molecular systems, DFT also extends its reach to mate-
rials science, elucidating the band structure and elec-
tronic properties of materials, thus shedding light on 
conductivity and optical behavior. Additionally, DFT 
facilitates the analysis of energy landscapes, providing 
derivatives of energy with respect to atomic positions, 
which in turn reveal critical points such as minimal 
and saddle points on potential energy surfaces. This 
understanding is fundamental for predicting reaction 
pathways and rates, thus bridging the gap between 
theoretical insight and practical applications in chemi-
cal and materials science.
Density functional theory
Density Functional Theory is a widely adopted quan-
tum mechanical framework for investigating the elec-
tronic structure of materials at the atomic scale. Within 
this formalism, the total energy of a many-electron 
system is expressed as a functional of the electron 
density, enabling an efficient yet accurate description 
of complex materials, including MXenes. In practice, 
DFT calculations are commonly performed using 
well-established computational packages such as the 
Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) [83– 85], 
which provides a robust platform for implementing 
various exchange–correlation approximations and 
treating periodic systems. A central aspect of DFT 
methodology is the classification of exchange–corre-
lation (XC) functionals, which largely determine the 
accuracy of calculated properties. These functions are 
typically organized in a hierarchical framework based 
on their level of approximation. The Local Spin Den-
sity Approximation (LSDA) represents the simplest 
level, where the XC energy depends solely on the local 
electron density and spin polarization [86]. Although 
computationally efficient, its applicability is limited in 
systems with strong density inhomogeneities.
The Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) 
improves upon LSDA by incorporating the gradient 
of the electron density, allowing for a more accurate 
description of structural, energetic, and electronic 
properties in a wide range of materials [87]. Further 
refinement is achieved with Meta-GGA functionals, 
which include higher-order terms such as kinetic 
energy density, enhancing the treatment of both 
localized and delocalized electrons [88]. At a more 
sophisticated level, Hybrid Functionals combine a 
portion of exact exchange from Hartree–Fock theory 
with conventional DFT approximations, significantly 
improving the prediction of band gaps, electronic 
structure, and charge-transfer behavior. These func-
tionals are further classified into Global Hybrids, 
Range-Separated Hybrids, Screened Hybrids, and 
Double-Hybrid approaches, depending on how 
exchange and correlation contributions are treated 
[89–91]. Such methods are particularly important for 
accurately describing transition metal-based systems 
and low-dimensional materials like MXenes. Within
